title: MSFT Stock Reverses to $530 as Investors Fear Lower Capex Might Signal the End of AI Bubble Despite Microsoft Beating Quarterly Earnings and Revenue Expectations - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock reversed sharply after initially jumping above $550 following strong quarterly results, as lower-than-expected capital expenditure intensified questions about infrastructure demand, future returns and whether excessive spending which has inflated the AI bubble will start to dry up. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares initially jumped above $550 after the company reported stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings and revenue, supported by accelerating cloud growth. However, the rally quickly reversed, sending the stock below $530 and toward $520 as investors reassessed the company’s infrastructure spending plans. The immediate concern was not a lack of demand but the scale and pace of Microsoft’s investment. Total capital expenditure and finance leases reached $45.2 billion, approximately 30% higher year over year but below analysts’ average estimate of $50.7 billion. The shortfall has raised questions about the timing of infrastructure expansion and the potential returns from the massive investments being made across the technology sector. With major companies committing billions of dollars to computing infrastructure, investors are increasingly concerned that spending expectations have become difficult to sustain. Microsoft reported net income of $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share, representing a 32% increase on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue increased to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, meeting Bloomberg’s analyst consensus estimate. Earnings comfortably exceeded expectations of $4.27 per share. The results demonstrate that Microsoft’s underlying business continues to expand despite growing scrutiny of its investment strategy. However, the market reaction suggests that strong financial performance alone may no longer be sufficient to sustain the stock’s upward momentum. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year, or 31% in constant currency. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella highlighted Microsoft’s efforts to improve computing capability, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, investors want evidence that strong demand will translate into attractive returns on infrastructure spending. Cloud growth remains a major strength, but the cost of expanding capacity could limit the financial benefits if revenue fails to keep pace with investment. Microsoft’s spending figures have become central to the debate over the sustainability of the technology rally. The company is expanding its computing infrastructure to support cloud services and growing demand for advanced computing, while other major technology companies are pursuing similarly expensive investment programmes. Elon Musk recently warned on X that more than 200 new cloud providers could face what he described as “guppy-level death and consolidation.” He argued that companies without substantial standalone revenue beyond data centres could struggle to secure financing in debt markets. His comments reflect broader concerns about whether infrastructure providers can generate sufficient revenue to justify their spending. If demand expectations weaken or financing becomes more expensive, companies with large commitments and limited cash generation could face significant pressure. For Microsoft, the issue is particularly important because investors have already priced in substantial future growth. Any indication that infrastructure demand is weaker than expected, or that returns are taking longer to materialise, could trigger further valuation adjustments. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months, climb above $550 earlier this week but slipped below $530 again. The price slip tested the 20 daily SMA in gray in September which has been acting as support. The $550 area represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone, revering lower. Microsoft’s stock has undergone a notable repricing in recent months, signaling a broader reset in how investors are assessing mega-cap technology leaders. After peaking above $555 in October 2025, shares retreated sharply, and despite the revival in 2026, buyers haven’t been able to break above that level. Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year over year. Search and advertising revenue, excluding traffic acquisition costs, increased 12%. However, Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, or 1% in constant currency, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22%. The contrasting performance highlights Microsoft’s dependence on its cloud business to sustain overall growth while some consumer-facing operations remain under pressure. Microsoft is developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce reliance on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually help Microsoft reduce computing costs. However, development and deployment require substantial investment, meaning the financial benefits will depend on successful implementation and sufficient demand. Microsoft has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, although the current status of those talks remains unclear. Microsoft faces additional pressure from the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority, which has proposed designating the company as having strategic market status in certain software markets. The designation could lead to greater scrutiny of licensing, pricing and product bundling. Competition from Google Workspace also presents challenges as businesses reassess Microsoft 365 costs and features. Meanwhile, restructuring in Microsoft’s gaming division, including planned job reductions, highlights efforts to improve efficiency across its operations. Microsoft’s earnings and cloud growth remain strong, but the reversal below $530 suggests investors are becoming more selective about expensive infrastructure investments. Buyers will need to demonstrate that the stock can regain momentum above $530 and challenge the $550 area again. Failure to recover could leave shares vulnerable to further selling toward $520 and potentially $500 if negative sentiment intensifies. The central question is whether Microsoft’s expanding infrastructure will generate sufficient revenue and cash flow to justify the investment. Until investors gain greater confidence in those returns, concerns about excessive spending and a potential AI bubble could continue to weigh on the stock.

Microsoft (MSFT) is the IBD Stock Of The Day after the software giant posted a beat-and-raise quarterly report highlighted by accelerating growth of cloud computing and artificial intelligence services. The Redmond, Wash.-based company late Wednesday said its fiscal first-quarter earnings rose 18% year over year to an adjusted $4.89 a share, topping analyst estimates for $4.71 a share. Sales increased 19% to $92.28 billion in the quarter ended Sept. 30, beating the target of $90.62 billion. Under the hood, the company's cloud and AI services performed even better. Microsoft's Azure cloud-computing business saw revenue increase 48% year over year in fiscal Q1, vs. 43% growth in previous quarter. Plus, it forecast Azure growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency for the current fiscal Q2. Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 30% year over year in the September quarter, accelerating from 27% growth in fiscal Q4. However, Microsoft stock dropped a fraction to close at 530.14 on the stock market today, amid an overall down day for megacaps and especially software. Earlier in the session, it rose as much as 1.9% to 541.29, flashing an aggressive entry, before retreating. Microsoft stock hit its 2026 high of 551.15 on Oct. 13. That followed its breakout from a cup base at a buy point of 466.32 on Aug. 3, according to IBD MarketSurge charts. The stock has forged an ascending base-like pattern with 551.15 as the buy point. Wednesday's intraday high of 535 is the early entry. At least 20 Wall Street analysts raised their price targets on Microsoft stock after the company's earnings report. Azure growth in the current quarter will be fueled by broad-based customer demand, sustained operational efficiency gains and ramping new data-center capacity, Stifel analyst Brad Reback said in a client note. He reiterated his buy rating on Microsoft stock and raised his price target to 650 from 575. Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives kept his outperform rating on Microsoft stock with a price target of 615. "We view Microsoft as the barometer for the enterprise in the AI revolution, and Azure's acceleration to 48% (growth), the 49% to 50% guide, and $677 billion of contracted backlog show enterprise AI spending at a pace that supports the capex behind it," Ives said in a report. BofA Securities analyst Tal Liani reiterated his buy rating on Microsoft stock and upped his price target to 630 from 600. "Microsoft's positioning across infrastructure, models and software continues to provide multiple paths to monetize AI demand," Liani said in a report. On a conference call with analysts, Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella noted growing adoption of the company's AI services, including its Copilot assistant. "We think of Copilot as the new OS (operating system) for work," Nadella said. "Customers are increasingly turning to Copilot to get real work done. Automated tasks have nearly doubled since July. Daily users are up nearly 50% quarter over quarter, and over 5X year over year." The number of customers paying for more than 50,000 Copilot seats is eight times higher than it was a year ago, he said. Plus, the number of Copilot customers actively consuming credits through usage-based billing grew over 75% over the quarter, Nadella said. title: Microsoft (MSFT Stock) Q1 FY2027 Earnings Show Azure Surging 48% as AI Raises Energy Concerns - CarbonCredits.com
content: Microsoft (MSFT stock) reported strong first-quarter results for fiscal 2027 as demand for artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and enterprise software continued to grow. Revenue reached $92.3 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up 19% year over year. Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion, highlighting the growing importance of AI infrastructure to its business. However, this expansion brings a major sustainability challenge. Microsoft’s 2026 Environmental Sustainability Report shows that its greenhouse gas emissions rose 25% in fiscal 2025 as the company expanded its data centers and changed how it procures renewable electricity. The results highlight a growing tension for the technology giant: scaling AI services while working toward its goal of becoming carbon negative by 2030. Microsoft’s first-quarter results show continued strength across its cloud and AI businesses. The company also reported commercial remaining performance obligations of $677 billion, up 73% year over year. This represents contracted revenue that Microsoft expects to recognize in the future, although the timing depends on customer demand and contract terms. Microsoft returned $10.2 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases during the quarter. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted the company’s technology capabilities, while CFO Amy Hood pointed to strong cloud growth and results that exceeded expectations for revenue, operating income, and earnings per share. Microsoft’s Agents and Infra segment generated $76.8 billion in revenue, up 25% year over year. Azure revenue increased 48% to $33.2 billion, while Microsoft 365 cloud revenue rose 17% to $27.8 billion. Industry solutions revenue increased 9% to $5.3 billion. Search and advertising revenue grew 10% to $6.6 billion. Other businesses showed mixed results. Windows OEM and devices revenue declined 22% to $3.6 billion, while Xbox revenue fell 2% to $5.4 billion. The Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion, down 3% year over year. These results show how cloud computing and AI are becoming central to the company’s growth. Microsoft shares (MSFT stock) gained more than 3% in after-hours trading following its October 28 earnings announcement, as Azure growth of 48% and stronger-than-expected results eased concerns about returns on AI infrastructure spending. The latest sustainability report shows that the company’s total greenhouse gas emissions increased 25% year over year. It attributed the rise mainly to expanding data-center infrastructure and its decision to stop using non-additional, unbundled renewable energy certificates as it prioritizes investments that bring new carbon-free electricity to power grids. This distinction matters. Renewable energy certificates can help companies account for renewable electricity, but they do not always lead to new clean energy generation. Microsoft is shifting toward projects and contracts intended to add new electricity supply. The latest report highlights the difficulty of reducing emissions while building data centers at speed. Microsoft’s climate strategy must address both the electricity used to operate its infrastructure and the carbon embedded in the materials and equipment required to expand it. Microsoft continues to improve data-center efficiency as demand for AI computing rises. Microsoft is also developing cooling technologies that reduce water demand. In its Phoenix data centers, cooling improvements delivered a 23% year-over-year reduction in WUE in FY2025. The company is extending similar improvements to other facilities. On clean electricity, it achieved its milestone of matching 100% of its annual global electricity consumption with renewable energy in FY2025. In February 2026, it reported that it had contracted 40 gigawatts of new renewable energy across 26 countries, with 19 GW already online. Matching electricity consumption with renewable energy is an important milestone, but it does not mean every data center runs entirely on renewable power at every hour. Grid conditions, project availability and the timing of electricity generation still matter. Microsoft also reported progress on water and waste. In FY2025, it replenished more than 14.2 million cubic meters of water, exceeding the amount it withdrew. The company achieved a 92% reuse and recycling rate for decommissioned cloud hardware, surpassing its 90% target for the second consecutive year. Reusing equipment and components can reduce waste and limit demand for new materials. Microsoft continues to invest in carbon removal as part of its plan to become carbon negative by 2030. Its 2026 report highlights an agreement with Rubicon Carbon to purchase up to 18 million metric tons of afforestation, reforestation and revegetation credits. These projects can help remove carbon from the atmosphere, but carbon removal alone cannot solve the emissions challenge. Microsoft must also reduce emissions from its operations, electricity purchases and supply chain. Microsoft’s latest earnings show that AI and cloud computing remain powerful growth drivers. Its sustainability report, however, shows that rising infrastructure demand continues to put pressure on its climate targets. For investors, the key question is whether Microsoft can improve efficiency, add new carbon-free electricity and cut supply-chain emissions fast enough to support its 2030 commitments. The company has made progress on renewable electricity, water replenishment and hardware reuse. Yet the 25% annual increase in emissions shows that its sustainability strategy faces a difficult test as AI infrastructure expands. title: The Memory Crunch Is Crushing Microsoft Windows PC Sales - 24/7 Wall St.
content: A global memory shortage is doing something no software competitor has managed: shrinking Microsoft's Windows business faster with each passing quarter, and the damage is spreading beyond PC makers into the data centers powering Microsoft's own AI ambitions. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) said on October 28, 2026, that its Windows business will shrink faster in the December quarter than in the September quarter it had just reported. The stock closed at $531.01 before the results. It then rose 2.90% to $546.39 in after-hours trading as of about 7:59 p.m. ET, because cloud strength offset the Windows warning. In this case, Windows sales means Windows OEM revenue, which is the license fees Microsoft collects from PC makers such as HP (NYSE:HPQ) and Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL). That revenue moves with PC unit sales. The memory shortage that is pressuring those PC makers also raises what Microsoft pays to build data centers. 2026's Biggest AI Trends: The Memory Explosion | MU Stock, SNDK Stock, SK Hynix, CAMT Stock Devices and Consumer revenue was $15.5 billion, and Windows OEM and devices revenue fell 22%. That roughly matched the low-20s decline CFO Amy Hood guided for on July 29, 2026. The Windows OEM line by itself missed. Amy Hood said it fell 27%, or 28% in constant currency (excluding exchange-rate moves), the same rate Counterpoint Research expects PC shipments to fall in the December quarter. She said it was “below expectations” and pointed to “the Windows 10 end of support demand in the prior year, inventory drawdowns by OEM and channel partners and weaker PC market demand.” The first cause is a tough comparison, since a year earlier buyers rushed to upgrade as Windows 10 support ended. For the December quarter, Amy Hood said “Windows OEM and devices revenue should decline in the mid-30s” and guided Devices and Consumer revenue to $15.9 billion to $16.4 billion. She added, “We expect these trends to continue through the rest of the fiscal year.” The link to memory comes from Hood’s earlier comments. In January 2026, she highlighted “the potential impact on the PC market from increased memory pricing,” and on July 29, she said partners were building inventory “given increasing component prices.” PC makers stocked up ahead of price hikes and are now selling down that inventory. That helps explain why Amy Hood’s guided decline deepened from the low 20s to the mid-30s. Ben Yeh, a principal analyst at Omdia, said memory’s share of PC costs has risen from roughly 15% to nearly 40%. That cost squeeze cut September-quarter PC shipments 21% to 57 million, Counterpoint Research counted, with HP falling 31% and Dell 25%; it expects another 27% drop in the December quarter. Its senior analyst, Minsoo Kang, said: “rising memory and component costs push system prices higher and force consumers to delay replacement purchases.” PC makers have been slipping, with HP down 3.37% to $32.45 in the October 28 regular session, and Dell slipped 1.63% to $493.79. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) rose 1.91% to $95.53, then dropped 2.55% to $93.09 after hours as of about 7:59 p.m. ET. Intel is expected to report on October 29, and HP and Dell are expected to report around November 24, although none of the three has confirmed its date. Amy Hood said about three-quarters of September-quarter capital spending went to short-lived assets, “primarily CPUs and GPUs, including higher memory and storage costs.” The same shortage that is cutting into Windows licensing also raises Microsoft’s data-center costs. Microsoft’s results still held up because Devices and Consumer is the smaller of its two segments. That data-center spending is going toward meeting AI demand from paying customers, and the suppliers wiring up those facilities, from power to cooling to networking, are the quieter beneficiaries of the same expansion (we covered seven of them in a free report on the AI infrastructure trade). A deeper Windows decline reduces a high-margin license stream, but it leaves the cloud business that drives Microsoft’s growth intact. A bottom in Windows would show up as partner inventories return to normal, memory prices ease, and the Windows 10 comparison drops out of the numbers. If the December-quarter earnings report shows Windows OEM and devices revenue falling further than Amy Hood’s mid-30s guide, the bullish case for Microsoft weakens. For Intel, the sore spot is the PC outlook, since Microsoft guided its Windows original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and devices revenue to decline by a percentage in the mid-30s in Q2 FY2027. That combination leaves Intel absorbing both AI spending worries and a weaker PC backdrop. Intel designs and manufactures its own chips, from Xeon server processors to Core Ultra PC chips, and wants to sell factory capacity on its 18A process to outside customers. Google runs search, YouTube and a fast-growing cloud on TPU silicon it designs in-house for its AI workloads. Microsoft rents out Azure capacity built on third-party graphics processing units and, increasingly, its own chip designs, and it’s a potential but unconfirmed Intel foundry customer. In this trio, Intel is the supplier hoping the other two turn into buyers. When Intel reports after the close, the key question is whether management can name new outside foundry customers. Intel’s Q2 2026 results offer some encouragement, with revenue growing 25.4% to $16.13 billion and data center and AI sales rising 59%. title: Microsoft Stock Has More Upside: Analyst Says Q1 Validation of ‘AI-Led Growth Opportunity’ - TradingView
content: Microsoft Corporation MSFT shares were trading lower Thursday after the company beat analyst estimates for its fiscal first quarter a day earlier. Here’s a look at what analysts liked about the earnings report and why most are raising their price targets on the stock. Scotiabank analyst Patrick Colville reiterated a Sector Outperform rating on Microsoft and raised the price target from $625 to $650. KeyBanc analyst Jackson Ader maintained an Overweight rating and raised the price target from $600 to $630. DA Davidson analyst Gil Luria reiterated a Buy rating and raised the price target from $550 to $650. Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Thomas Blakey maintained an Overweight rating and raised the price target from $608 to $630. JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee reiterated an Overweight rating with a price target of $625. Azure growth was the key highlight for Colville in the first quarter. The analyst also highlighted the company’s lighter than expected capex. "Based on our short-lived capex analysis, we estimate Azure can grow in an upside case 54% in 2Q," Colville said. Colville highlighted Microsoft receiving more than $2.50 in incremental AI revenue for every $1 of AI depreciation. "We see this print as evidence that the company is a leading horseman of the AI revolution." Azure, Copilot and Capex were the three focus areas for Ader in results and they all outperformed. "The three key areas that we are focused on all showed meaningful upside, and the momentum in those areas is expected to continue for the remainder of the year," Ader said. Luria sees Microsoft’s first quarter having wins for both the software and infrastructure AI offerings. "Copilot continued to gain adoption, and Azure continued to show accelerating growth," Luria said. The analyst said Microsoft expects to remain free cash flow positive despite its large capex spending. Azure accelerating despite capacity constraints was the highlight from the first quarter for Blakey. "We view the quarter as further validation of Microsoft’s AI-led growth opportunity, while continuing to monitor capacity delivery timing, cloud margin pressure from Azure mix and component costs inflation, and the ability to sustain infrastructure returns as investment accelerates," Blakey said The analyst expects Microsoft to be a "leading beneficiary" for AI intelligence in the enterprise sector. "With AI investment continuing to scale, we are watching whether efficiency gains and improved monetization can increasingly offset infrastructure costs and support margin stabilization over time." Chatterjee highlights Azure acceleration and Microsoft’s capital needs being favorable to peers after Q1 results. "Microsoft delivered a print and outlook that should reinforce the bull thesis around compute efficiencies supporting a broad-based acceleration in growth," Chatterjee said. The analyst said the strong numbers and forward upside show Microsoft’s ability to balance its compute allocation across multiple growth drivers. Microsoft shares were down 1.4% to $523.48 on Thursday versus a 52-week trading range of $349.20 to $551.15. Shares traded higher in the earlier trading session before declining. title: New Microsoft Price Target as $33 Billion Cloud Update Turns Heads - RealMoney Pro
content: Waiting for answers on 2027 free cash flow and capex questions could keep the shares capped near term. Microsoft (MSFT) delivered the kind of quarter investors have been waiting for from the AI buildout: accelerating cloud growth, guidance ahead of expectations and better than expected free cash flow that more than doubled what Wall Street had modeled. Coming into the company’s earnings call, we shared that we knew we had some catch up work to do with our MSFT price target. That combined with what we saw and heard on Wednesday night is leading us to boost that target to $600 from $500. Others across Wall Street are taking their MSFT targets higher, in some cases meaningfully higher. Wells Fargo reset its target at $750, and Citi is now at $680, while Morgan Stanley landed at $650. The key behind our price target and most likely those other ones is that Azure continues to deliver meaningful upside relative to market expectations despite capacity constraints. Azure revenue grew 48% to $33.2 billion versus the 44% Wall Street expected, and management guided for growth to pick up to 49% to 50% in the December quarter even with some third-party capacity slipping into 2027, because demand continues to exceed supply. Microsoft’s commercial backlog jumped 73% to $677 billion, equal to roughly 10.6 quarters of the $63.9 billion in Microsoft Cloud revenue it booked in the September quarter. Similar to what we saw with Q3 2026 results for Google’s (GOOGL) cloud segment, the operating income at Microsoft’s operating income for Agents and Infra rose at a brisker pace compared to its revenue. But the big difference between the two is the $18.6 billion in free cash flow Microsoft delivered versus the roughly $8.5 billion Wall Street modeled, while still returning $10.2 billion to shareholders. That said, like Meta (META), Google, and most likely as we’ll hear on Thursday from Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft expects to step up its capex spend in calendar 2027. This more than likely means Wall Street will need to revisit its free cash flow expectations for Microsoft when the company reports its current quarter in early January and lays out its calendar 2027 capex plans. Until we have greater clarity on that, and whether that free cash flow figure is a positive one or not and how its stacks up against Wall Street expectations, we are keeping our Two rating in play. Current consensus expectations have Microsoft delivering free cash flow near $30 billion in the current fiscal year that ends June 2027 and $35.6 billion for the one ending June 2028. Even though we can see upside to $600 for MSFT shares, waiting the answer to that question could keep MSFT shares range bound. Should Microsoft tap its investments in OpenAI and Databricks following IPOs for those companies, that would lead us, and most likely others, to revisit capex spend and potential cash flow dynamics. It would also have a role to play in revisiting our new MSFT target price. Before we move on to discuss Microsoft’s quarter, we’ll reiterate one of the comments we made regarding Google and eventual cash flow. When Microsoft’s AI buildout begins to temper and capex starts to decline, it stands to reason that Azure margins will lift and the company’s free cash flow reaccelerates. That’s the medium- to longer-term opportunity in the shares. For its fiscal first quarter of 2027, Microsoft’s revenue climbed 19% to $92.3 billion, ahead of the 17% growth and $90.6 billion analysts expected, and adjusted EPS of $4.89 topped the $4.71 consensus. What stands out to us is the operating leverage. Operating income rose 21% while operating expenses grew just 6%, and operating margin edged up to 50%. CFO Amy Hood credited efficiency gains across the GPU and CPU fleet that let Microsoft sell more capacity without adding cost, and that’s where internal AI use shows up in the numbers: throughput for Copilot workloads rose more than 50% from the June quarter, and in-house AI models are taking on more work at lower cost. Under the new segment structure, Agents and Infra revenue grew 25% to $76.8 billion, Microsoft Cloud revenue accelerated to 30% growth and Foundry revenue more than tripled. M365 commercial cloud grew 18% in constant currency on an adjusted basis, helped by GitHub Copilot, and management expects about 19% growth in the December quarter with acceleration through the fiscal year. The soft spot remains Devices and Consumer, where revenue fell 3% to $15.5 billion and Windows OEM and devices revenue is expected to fall in the mid-30% range in the December quarter on elevated PC inventory and a tough Windows 10 comparison. That Device and Consumer outlook should not be a surprise given the Q3 2026 drop in PC industry shipments. On the customer AI side, Microsoft is seeing adoption broaden. Copilot daily users rose nearly 50% from the June quarter and more than five-times year over year, the number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats rose more than eight times, and the number of customers consuming Copilot credits through usage-based billing grew more than 75%. That shift from per-seat subscriptions to consumption expands Microsoft’s addressable market, though Hood cautioned it will move more slowly outside of coding. Those data points and others support the view that AI adoption is rising and usage expanding, and that reinforces our position on several holdings in the Portfolio that stand to benefit from the AI infrastructure build out as does the collective step up in AI and data center capex. For the December quarter, Microsoft guided revenue to $96.0 billion to $97.1 billion, above the $95.6 billion consensus, with operating margin down slightly year over year as Azure becomes a bigger part of the mix and costs from its latest employee buyout offer flow through. Capital spending for the quarter came in at $45.2 billion, below Microsoft’s own $50 billion forecast, largely because third-party capacity deliveries slipped, not because Microsoft pulled back. Still, that likely means Microsoft would have still delivered positive free cash flow for the quarter, more likely in-line with what Wall Street had forecasted. The larger question is It expects capex to top $50 billion in the December quarter, total about $170 billion for calendar 2026 and accelerate again in the first half of 2027 as those deliveries arrive and memory and storage costs climb. That along with Meta’s (META) step up in capex bodes well for Arista Networks (ANET) but as we’ve discussed capacity constraints could make for fits and starts for Arista’s deliverables. Microsoft added 24 new data centers across five continents in the quarter, installed its first Nvidia (NVDA) Vera Rubin GPUs and cut the time it takes to bring new GB300 capacity online by about 20%. Operating cash flow rose 29% to $58 billion, and capex consumed about 68% of it, compared with roughly 122% at Alphabet, which is why Microsoft generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow while Alphabet burned $9.1 billion. Granted, some of Microsoft’s upside is capex timing, and let’s remember it also leans on finance leases, $7.4 billion in the quarter, that don’t run through that cash figure. Even so, management expects to remain free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027 and will tap leasing or debt markets only “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” As we called out above, come January we’ll have a better indication for that free cash flow figure and how it stacks up against Wall Street’s models. At the time of publication, TheStreet Pro was long AMZN, ANET, GOOGL, META, MSFT and NVDA. BY James "Rev Shark" DePorre · Oct 29, 2026, 4:35 PM EDT

title: Satya Nadella Says Renting AI Capacity to a Few Big Customers Is “Not a Business” - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Satya Nadella drew a sharp line between the AI customers Microsoft wants and the ones it will tolerate, and the distinction reveals something uncomfortable about how the biggest names in cloud infrastructure actually make their money. On the September-quarter earnings call of Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction), held October 28, 2026, Satya Nadella compared the enterprise customers he wants with “like 4 customers who buy a lot of capacity from you and you can show a few quarters of growth.” He added, “And that’s not a business as far as I’m concerned.” The remark came from results in which Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19%, with Azure revenue up 48%. Shares closed at $531.01 before the release, down 0.06%, leaving the company worth $3.94 trillion. After the call, they traded at $546.39 at about 7:59 p.m. ET, up 2.90%. Microsoft (MSFT) The Least Magnificent of the Mag 7 - Time To Sell? A Bernstein Research analyst asked how much of Azure’s AI demand comes from enterprises. Satya Nadella said Rolls-Royce runs jet-engine maintenance across 30,000 parts on Foundry, Microsoft’s platform for building AI agents, and that Austrian bank RBI showed him 20-plus business processes end to end. These are recurring workflows that use compute every day, so they last longer than a one-time capacity purchase. Nadella did not name any company. He said Microsoft is “open for business” with large buyers because “as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some.” Nadella told Morgan Stanley’s Adam Wood that “we have one pool and we want to get the pool to be as efficient and fungible.” Fungible capacity is hardware that can shift among many customers and workloads, which lowers the risk that one departing buyer leaves expensive chips idle. Amy Hood said capex of $45.2 billion came in below her July 29 guide of over $50 billion “as some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed.” She added that “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply.” For the December quarter, Amy Hood guided Azure growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency and capex of over $50 billion, with calendar-year spending of approximately $170 billion. A company that is short on supply can afford to be choosy on price, so the stance costs Microsoft little. Commercial remaining performance obligation, which is contracted revenue not yet recognized, rose 73% to $677 billion, while commercial bookings fell 12%. Hood tied the decline to “large Azure commitments in the prior year,” partly offset by “a large Azure commitment this quarter.” Microsoft also recorded $10.0 billion of revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI out of $92.279 billion, or about 10.8%. It also buys third-party capacity, so it sits on both sides of the model Nadella questioned. For comparison, CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) closed at $63.93 on October 28. For the June 2026 quarter, it reported three unnamed customers at 36%, 26% and 10% of revenue. Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) closed at $144.54 with $638 billion of remaining performance obligations. S&P Global Ratings (SGR) estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of that total. Microsoft’s results support its growth case. Demand is running ahead of supply, so capacity is what limits revenue, and the growing backlog shows customers are signing commitments years in advance. The risks are heavy capex, delayed third-party deliveries, and the share of revenue that comes from OpenAI. Spreading AI across many enterprise workflows is how Microsoft reduces that concentration over time, and this quarter showed that spread growing. All of that capex has to be powered and cooled by somebody, which is why the suppliers behind the data centers keep showing up alongside the hyperscalers themselves. We pulled together seven of them in a free report on the AI infrastructure buildout. Microsoft has not confirmed the date of its next report. If Azure growth falls short of Amy Hood’s 49% to 50% guidance, or OpenAI’s share of revenue rises above about 10.8%, the case for breadth gets weaker. title: OpenAI Now Makes Up 11% of Microsoft’s Revenue - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Microsoft's latest quarterly filing reveals it partly owns one of its biggest customers, and the money flowing between them is growing faster than most investors realize. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) filed its quarterly report for the three months ended September 30 with the SEC on October 28, 2026. It shows $10.0 billion of revenue from OpenAI, out of total revenue of $92.279 billion at Microsoft. That is about 10.8%, which means Microsoft partly owns one of its largest customers. The stock closed at $531.01, down 0.06%. After hours, it rose 2.90% to $546.39 as of about 7:59 p.m. ET. OpenAI revenue helps justify Microsoft’s data center expansion, but it also links more of the payback to one private customer that needs a lot of cash. The filing calls the figure “revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, inclusive of revenue-sharing payments,” so it covers more than Azure cloud purchases. Microsoft reports it because OpenAI is an equity-method investee, meaning Microsoft owns enough of it to count its share of OpenAI’s results, and that makes OpenAI a related party. Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges rounded the share to 11% on the earnings call, telling CEO Satya Nadella, “you have OpenAI at 11% of revenue in the quarter.” Microsoft itself did not give that number. In fiscal 2026, OpenAI was about 7.3% of revenue: $24.1 billion out of $331.839 billion. The September quarter alone produced roughly 41% of that full-year total. OpenAI owed Microsoft $7.2 billion at September 30, up from $6.0 billion at June 30. That is a 20% rise in three months. Receivables are bills sent but not yet paid, so this rise means Microsoft is giving more trade credit to a company it partly owns. Microsoft holds “an approximate 24% interest on an as-converted basis,” down from about 25% at June 30. It has paid $12.0 billion of its $13.0 billion commitment. Hood put calendar 2026 spending at approximately $170 billion, slightly below her July 29 guidance of about $175 billion. Free cash flow was $18.6 billion, and Hood expects it to stay positive through fiscal 2027. Microsoft’s fundamentals look solid. content: Shares of AI infrastructure providers tumbled Thursday pre-market after Microsoft Corp. MSFT and Alphabet Inc. GOOG GOOGL reported quarterly capital spending below Wall Street expectations, reviving concerns about the pace as well as sustainability of hyperscaler spending that has fueled the artificial intelligence boom. CoreWeave Inc. CRWV fell about 5% in Thursday’s pre-market trade, Nebius Group NV NBIS dropped 6%, IREN Ltd. IREN declined 4% and Applied Digital Corp. APLD slid 4%, according to Benzinga Pro data. CoreWeave had been on track for its best week in 11 weeks, while Nebius was heading toward its strongest weekly performance in 10 weeks. IREN was similarly on pace for its best week in seven weeks, while Applied Digital had been headed for its strongest week in 23 weeks. The sharp reversal highlights how sensitive the neocloud trade has become to signals from the largest AI infrastructure spenders. The selloff came after Microsoft and Alphabet both reported quarterly capital spending below Wall Street expectations. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases for the quarter, roughly 30% higher than a year earlier but below the $50.7 billion average analyst estimate, according to StreetAccount as cited by CNBC. Alphabet also came in below expectations, reporting $51.36 billion in capital expenditures versus the $55.09 billion analysts had expected. While both companies continue to spend enormous sums on AI infrastructure, the misses have raised questions about whether hyperscalers can sustain the explosive pace of spending that has underpinned demand for neocloud providers. The concerns come as investors are already questioning the financing model behind the AI infrastructure boom. Market commentator Nicholas Mugalli recently warned that data-center delays and soaring construction costs could create an existential challenge for highly leveraged neocloud operators. Microsoft, meanwhile, traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants’ latest spending and free cash flow numbers in the third-quarter earnings report. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive. The earnings reports come as investors scrutinize AI spending plans of tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments. “Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises,” Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday. “Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call” . Alphabet’s biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company’s shares. Philipp Schindler, Alphabet’s chief business officer, said the impact on the search business was partly because of lower monetization within the company’s AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now “scaling” ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets. Google’s search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google’s own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace. “The problem for Google is it faces an innovator’s dilemma and doesn’t know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI,” Barringer said. Google’s dominant market share in the search business, however, could ultimately give it a leg up over its peers, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt said. “I don’t think it’s a sea change,” Devitt told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” on Thursday. “If it’s a problem for Alphabet, it’s a problem for any consumer-facing AI agent or LLM as well. And so, it’s a problem that I think is ultimately going to be resolved. And when it does, Alphabet, with its 4 billion search customers that become AI customers, is in an enviable position.” - CNBC’s Robert Hum, Samantha Subin, Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed reporting. A: CEO Satya Nadella emphasized that enterprise breadth is starting to materialize, with customers like Unilever and Rolls-Royce building complex agentic systems on Foundry. Microsoft shares popped after hours while Alphabet stock sank. Why? I think a big part of the answer is how each plans to pay for the massive outlays both have planned. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Microsoft beat Wall Street's targets with sales up 19%, reaching $92.3 billion. GAAP -- generally accepted accounting principles -- earnings per share (EPS) came in at $4.92. Adjusted EPS was $4.89, above the roughly $4.72 the Street expected. Azure, its cloud platform, grew 48%, reaching $33.17 billion in revenue. Alphabet's cloud growth was even stronger than Microsoft's: 103% growth for the unit, earning $11.1 billion in operating income on $30.7 billion in sales. Overall, sales jumped 25%, reaching $127.6 billion, slightly missing estimates, while GAAP EPS actually fell from $2.87 to $2.12. Search and YouTube ads also underperformed. Some of Alphabet's EPS drop can be explained by an $8.7 billion net loss on equity securities, but even if you remove this -- worth $0.55 per share -- the earnings still came in well below what Wall Street was looking for. While it's not a great look, I think the real issue the market is reacting to is the company's cash picture. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures (capex), up from $24.0 billion a year ago. Operating cash flow -- the cash the actual business generated -- was $42.3 billion. That left free cash flow (FCF) -- the money left after paying for its capex investments -- at negative $9.1 billion. That's worse than the negative $5.9 billion the company reported last quarter. During the quarter, Alphabet raised $28.7 billion through senior unsecured notes and $12.4 billion from selling stock. Long-term debt has grown from $46.5 billion at the end of 2025 to $125.1 billion. Alphabet said its capex guidance for 2026 holds -- $195 billion to $205 billion -- but said it expects capex in 2027 to "increase significantly." Microsoft, on the other hand, is still FCF positive, though like Alphabet, that figure is moving in the wrong direction. The company reported FCF of $18.63 billion, down 27% year over year, after $39.37 billion in cash capital spending. Its broader capex figure, which includes finance leases, was $45.2 billion. CFO Amy Hood said on July's earnings call that the company expects to stay free-cash-flow positive for its current fiscal year, though capex is expected to expand. On that call, she also said demand for its cloud services was running ahead of supply. Microsoft at this point has a much healthier cushion in its quarterly cash flow -- more room to keep spending while it waits for those investments to pay off. Alphabet is increasingly asking lenders and shareholders to help cover the bill. Obviously, the growth is hard to argue with, but I still think the jury is out on whether this bet will pay off for both companies. Costs are climbing, and I'm concerned the math won't pencil out long term. title: MSFT Stock Jumps Above $550 Ahead of Fiscal First-Quarter Earnings as Microsoft Spending Concerns Mount - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock jumped above $550 after the fiscal Q1 earnings report, as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have pulled back toward $525 after failing to establish a new record above $550. The reversal follows a rally supported by news of the company’s custom-chip development, but investors are now weighing the potential returns from Microsoft’s expanding infrastructure commitments against rising competitive and regulatory risks. The company reports fiscal first-quarter earnings today, October 28, putting its cloud business, profitability and capital expenditure plans under close scrutiny. Despite strong historical earnings growth, buyers need evidence that Microsoft’s investment strategy can deliver sustainable returns without placing excessive pressure on cash generation. Microsoft reported net income of $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share, for the quarter, representing a 32% increase on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, while Wall Street had expected earnings of $4.27 per share and revenue of $90.6 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year, or 31% in constant currency. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share, highlighting a strong start to the fiscal year. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said Microsoft was delivering greater computing capability, customer choice and cost efficiency, while focusing on security and helping organisations develop their own AI capabilities. Revenue from Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment fell 3% to $15.5 billion, reflecting weakness across several businesses. Search and advertising revenue, excluding traffic acquisition costs, increased 12%. However, Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, or 1% in constant currency, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue dropped 22%. The contrasting results highlight continued cloud strength alongside weaker demand in parts of Microsoft’s consumer and hardware businesses. Microsoft’s financial performance remains robust. Fiscal 2026 revenue increased 18% to $331.8 billion, while net income climbed 31% to $133.7 billion. However, the cost of supporting its cloud and computing expansion is becoming increasingly important to investors. Capital expenditure reached $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, with approximately two-thirds directed toward shorter-lived CPUs and GPUs. Operating cash flow totalled $55.4 billion, while free cash flow stood at $19.6 billion. Capital expenditure is expected to remain above $50 billion per quarter during fiscal 2027. These commitments raise questions about how quickly Microsoft’s revenue can expand to justify the spending. Even with strong demand, the company must demonstrate that its infrastructure investments can generate attractive returns rather than simply increasing operating capacity at considerable cost. Microsoft is developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce reliance on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually help Microsoft control computing costs, although development, deployment and infrastructure expansion require substantial upfront investment. The company has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, according to The Information, although the current status of those talks remains unclear. SpaceX expects to finish 2026 with slightly more than 2 gigawatts of computing capacity and aims to expand to between 5 GW and 10 GW next year. Microsoft’s continued capacity constraints highlight the scale of the challenge, even as spending accelerates. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months, climb above $550 earlier this week but slipped below $530 again. The price slip tested the 20 daily SMA in gray in September which has been acting as support. The $550 area represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone. Microsoft’s stock has undergone a notable repricing in recent months, signaling a broader reset in how investors are assessing mega-cap technology leaders. After peaking above $555 in October 2025, shares retreated sharply, and despite the revival in 2026, buyers haven’t been able to break above that level. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has concluded an investigation launched in May 2026 into Microsoft’s software business, including Word, Excel and Teams. The watchdog believes Microsoft should receive a strategic market status designation, potentially allowing greater regulatory scrutiny and targeted interventions. The CMA has raised concerns about the difficulty customers may face when switching providers, Microsoft’s position among approximately 20 million UK users and the competitive implications of its Copilot offering. The proposed designation does not establish wrongdoing. However, additional oversight could increase compliance costs and place restrictions on pricing, licensing or product-bundling strategies. Microsoft also faces intensifying competition from Google Workspace as businesses reassess Microsoft 365 pricing and bundled features. Maintaining its position in productivity software will require continued innovation while protecting margins. Meanwhile, the company is restructuring its gaming division, with approximately 3,200 job reductions planned during fiscal 2027, including 1,600 immediate cuts. The reductions reflect efforts to improve efficiency as Microsoft manages costs across its broader operations.

title: Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat - CNBC
content:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business. Here’s how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus: Microsoft’s revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement, with Azure now its biggest single business. The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion. With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue. For Azure, Microsoft’s finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts that she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus. “We still have demand that exceeds supply,” she said. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. “Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed,” Hood said. Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft’s prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue. Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues. “In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2,” she said. The delays have to do with GPU-as-a-service providers, she said. Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time. Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it’s attractive to do so, Hood said. “We’re fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven’t been able to — we haven’t yet, I would say, tapped that,” she said. “And then, of course, there’s other options.” Microsoft’s net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI. For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%. Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses. In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services. The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said. Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers. Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand. As of Wednesday’s close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs, and followed up by announcing on Monday that it’s offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. We came across a bullish thesis on Amazon.com, Inc. on Quality Stocks | GARP Investment Research's Substack. Since the thesis was published on August 26th, AMZN shares have edged lower amid concerns that heavy AI infrastructure spending could pressure near-term cash flow, creating a short-term headwind while strong AWS growth supports the long-term case. In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on AMZN. Amazon.com, Inc.'s share was trading at $253.10 as of October 27th 2026. AMZN's trailing and forward P/E were 20.04 and 23.10 respectively according to Yahoo Finance. This isn't the first time we see a technology company pitched as a great investment. AMZN shares gained 9.90% over the last 12 months. Comparable stocks like Alphabet gained 16.76% during the same period. Why are technology stocks rising, and does AMZN's slower climb leave room for it to catch up? In July, we published an article about the 12 Best Dow Stocks to Invest In Right Now and AMZN ranked 1st in that article. AMZN has gained modestly since then, keeping the bullish call in positive territory but giving investors little to celebrate so far. This article explains why hedge funds were bullish on AMZN. Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much. Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) operates one of the largest consumer, cloud computing, advertising, and logistics ecosystems in the world. Its investment case increasingly depends on AWS, artificial intelligence infrastructure, advertising, and a shift toward higher-margin businesses rather than traditional e-commerce. Sales growth has been strong and steady, rising 12% in 2024 and an estimated 15% in 2025, with a similar pace expected in 2026 as Amazon.com, Inc. moves toward $1 trillion in annual revenue. Read More: 15 AI Stocks That Are Quietly Making Investors Rich Read More: Undervalued AI Stock Poised For Massive Gains: 10000% Upside Potential AWS alone generated $45.6 billion in operating income in 2025, underlining how central cloud computing has become to the company's profits. The stock trades around 21 times earnings at $262 per share, a multiple that rises closer to 30 times once one-time, non-operating gains are stripped out — a reminder that investors are really paying for future AWS growth, AI monetization, and margin improvement rather than today's reported earnings. The bullish case rests on several growth engines reinforcing one another. Higher-margin segments such as AWS, advertising, third-party seller services, and subscriptions are letting profits grow faster than overall sales. Online retail is still the biggest source of revenue for Amazon.com, Inc., but advertising and third-party services are more profitable, while AWS remains both the company's main earnings driver and its gateway into the AI boom. As more companies increase spending on AI infrastructure, AWS stands to benefit from rising demand for computing power, storage, databases, and AI tools such as Amazon Bedrock, opening up a fresh growth cycle for the business. The AI ambitions of Amazon.com, Inc. go beyond AWS. The company is also applying artificial intelligence to warehouse automation, logistics, advertising targeting, product recommendations, and tools that help third-party sellers run their businesses more efficiently. AWS's growth rate has accelerated sharply, from 18% to 35%, a sign that Amazon.com, Inc. remains competitive even as Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud post faster growth of their own. Even so, the company still has to prove that its heavy AI investments will generate strong returns and turn into durable earnings growth (see whether Amazon's custom AI chips can outpace its capital spending). Operating leverage is a key part of the investment case, as Amazon.com, Inc. shifts toward more profitable businesses and becomes more efficient across its operations. Management expects capital spending of around $200 billion in 2026, mostly for AI infrastructure, data centers, and chips — spending large enough to push free cash flow into negative territory. Bulls see this as growth investment rather than routine maintenance spending, but it also means Amazon.com, Inc. needs strong AWS growth and sustained AI demand to justify spending at this scale over the coming years. The revenue mix of Amazon.com, Inc. is steadily shifting toward higher-value services. Advertising, third-party seller services, subscriptions, and AWS are becoming a larger part of the business relative to lower-margin first-party retail. This shift matters because it lets profits grow faster than revenue as these segments gain a bigger share of the overall mix. Based on this trajectory, expected returns work out to roughly 12.1% annualized, driven by organic growth, expanding margins, and an overall improvement in business quality. On valuation, the stock already reflects a good deal of optimism. A base-case fair value estimate puts shares of Amazon.com, Inc. around $251, with a bull-case scenario reaching $305 if revenue growth and operating margins come in stronger than expected. At current levels, the stock doesn't look dramatically overvalued, but it also doesn't offer much of a safety cushion, since investors are already paying up for faster AWS growth, AI-driven gains, and improving profitability. If AI spending falls short of expectations, AWS growth slows, or operating leverage disappoints, the premium built into the stock could come under pressure. The biggest risk to this thesis is that AI demand may stay concentrated among a small number of large customers, even as it requires enormous upfront investment. The $200 billion capital spending plan of Amazon.com, Inc. could pay off handsomely if cloud demand keeps accelerating, but weaker AI adoption, pricing pressure, or slower monetization could leave the company with high infrastructure costs and limited profit growth. Competition across cloud computing, advertising, retail, logistics, and AI — along with regulatory scrutiny — adds further uncertainty to the long-term picture. Another risk for the stock is disruption to the systems that support AWS and Amazon's wider operations. Customers rely on these services to keep applications, payments, and business processes running, making reliability central to the cloud franchise. Amazon warns that system failures or security incidents can interrupt services, cause data loss, and expose it to liability. A prolonged outage could disrupt customers and require costly remediation. Repeated incidents could also weaken confidence and make businesses more cautious about placing additional workloads on AWS. These pressures could hurt growth and profitability even if demand for AI computing remains strong. In our opinion, Amazon's premium valuation becomes harder to defend if reliability problems undermine its main earnings engine. Hedge fund positioning shows a strong signal for Amazon.com, Inc. As per our database, 369 hedge fund portfolios held the stock at the end of the second quarter, up from 353 in the previous quarter. This steady rise in institutional ownership suggests hedge funds remained constructive on Amazon.com, Inc.'s AWS growth, AI opportunity, advertising business, and long-term margin expansion potential. By comparison, Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) was held by 273 hedge fund portfolios, down from 282, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) was held by 195 hedge funds, down from 201, and Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) was held by 119 hedge funds, up from 115. The rise in ownership of Amazon.com, Inc. and Oracle Corporation, against declines for Microsoft Corporation and Alphabet Inc., points to relatively stronger institutional conviction toward Amazon.com, Inc. during the period, even as funds continue weighing its premium valuation and heavy AI spending against its long-term growth potential. Short interest data also paints a fairly calm picture for Amazon.com, Inc. relative to its peers. About 0.88% of Amazon.com, Inc.'s float is sold short, slightly higher than Microsoft Corporation at 0.82%, but below Alphabet Inc. at 1.37% and well below Oracle Corporation at 2.60%. This suggests Amazon.com, Inc. is drawing similarly limited skepticism to Microsoft Corporation, while bearish bets remain less aggressive than those against Alphabet Inc. and Oracle Corporation, even as investors weigh its valuation and capital spending. AMZN's forward P/E is 23.10x. Microsoft Corporation, Oracle Corporation, and Alphabet Inc. trade at forward P/Es of 26.88x, 15.54x, and 20.24x, respectively. AMZN's own forward P/E was 22.96x on December 31, 2025, making its current valuation approximately 0.6% higher. We believe the current valuation reflects expectations for AWS growth, advertising expansion, and improving margins, balanced against concerns about heavy AI spending and uncertain investment returns. However, the valuation appears reasonable rather than deeply discounted, as Amazon trades below Microsoft but above Oracle and Alphabet. AWS generated $45.6 billion in operating income in 2025, while Amazon's approximately $200 billion capital spending plan for 2026 underscores how much future growth depends on earning adequate returns from new infrastructure. We believe AMZN can justify its current valuation if higher-margin businesses sustain earnings growth while absorbing rising depreciation and financing costs. If Amazon maintains its cloud momentum and successfully turns AI investment into lasting profits and cash flow, the current valuation could offer a reasonable entry point despite the risks surrounding its infrastructure expansion. Previously, we covered a bullish thesis on Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN) by FluentInQuality in May 2025, which highlighted AWS growth, logistics infrastructure, Prime ecosystem, advertising strength, and Amazon's five interconnected category leaders. AMZN's stock price has appreciated by approximately 23.16% since our coverage. We believe AMZN is a reasonable long-term investment if AWS and other higher-margin businesses turn its AI spending into sustained earnings and cash flow, though the current valuation leaves limited room for execution missteps. Amazon.com, Inc. is on our list of the 40 Most Popular Stocks Among Hedge Funds. The options market is pricing in a move of about $26, or roughly 5% of the notional value of the stock, which would put the expected range near $505 to $560 and would take MSFT through its 52-week high on the upside. History says to respect the tails. MSFT’s actual move exceeded the implied move in four of the last eight reports, including a 16% surge in April 2025 and a 13.4% jump last July. What's interesting is that the December 2026 cycle still has about 2x more implied volatility on a notional level, with a +-$46 implied range, so there is still some implied volatility priced in through the end of the year. Azure remains the engine of the story. Microsoft’s cloud platform grew 43% in fiscal Q4 and crossed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time, and management has guided to 44% to 45% growth this quarter. Intelligent Cloud revenue is guided to $40.95 billion to $41.25 billion, up 33% to 34%. One wrinkle to watch: Microsoft re-segmented its reporting in September, so Azure growth is now measured under an updated definition. The backlog is the other headline number. Commercial RPO, the contracted revenue not yet recognized, hit $678 billion last quarter. Excluding OpenAI, it still grew 25%, which matters because concentration risk with OpenAI has been a persistent concern since early this year. Management has also said repeatedly that demand continues to exceed available capacity, so Azure growth is a function of how fast Microsoft can bring GPUs and data centers online. Capital spending is where the bull and bear debates collide. Microsoft spent $41 billion on capex in fiscal Q4, roughly two thirds on short-lived assets like GPUs and CPUs, and has guided to more than $50 billion this quarter. Calendar 2026 capex is expected to land near $175 billion. Heavy depreciation has already pressured margins: gross margin slipped to 67.6% in fiscal Q3, the lowest since 2022, and cloud gross margin was 65% last quarter. Microsoft still guided operating margin roughly flat year over year, so any slippage there will draw attention. The macro backdrop adds pressure. AI-linked stocks sold off on October 8 after a report that OpenAI’s revenue was lower than expected, and again on October 22, when MSFT fell 2.2%. Anthropic filed for its IPO on October 26, and Meta has outlined up to $95 billion in equity financing, keeping the question of how the AI buildout gets funded front and center. The bull case starts with momentum in estimates and demand. Analysts have nudged revenue estimates higher by about 1% over the past three months, with the biggest upward revisions concentrated in Intelligent Cloud, and Microsoft has a track record of beating on EPS, including a nearly 12% surprise last quarter ($4.74 versus $4.24). Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats, up from 20 million one quarter earlier, with net seat additions more than doubling. Management is also adding usage-based billing for Copilot products, which could widen monetization. Sentiment on the Street is constructive: 43 of 49 analysts rate MSFT a Buy, the consensus price target is about $592, and Oppenheimer, Scotiabank, and Truist all lifted targets this week, with two of them going to $625. Bulls also point to Microsoft’s diversified AI exposure, including its roughly 27% stake in OpenAI and a relationship with Anthropic that includes both an investment and a large Azure commitment. A beat-and-raise on Azure with stable margins would give the stock a path through $553.72 into price discovery. Bears argue that MSFT is priced for a clean beat. The stock is up about 36% in three months, and the technical picture is less convincing than the headline: MSFT has stalled three times near $546, and momentum indicators have shown bearish divergence. The January report is the cautionary tale, when shares fell as much as 12% intraday after capex jumped 66% and Microsoft disclosed that roughly 45% of its RPO was tied to OpenAI. This time, more than $50 billion in quarterly capex, falling gross margins, and nervousness about AI financing could easily outweigh a strong Azure print. Weakness outside the cloud is another drag, with More Personal Computing revenue down 4% and Xbox content and services down 5% in the last report. If Azure comes in at the low end of guidance or management signals higher spending without a matching revenue lift, a stock sitting near its highs has a long way to fall.
